questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a version control system?

options.B: To track changes to files over time and allow reverting to earlier versions
options.C: To automatically fix bugs in your code
options.D: To share files between computers via email

questions.explanation: Version control systems (VCS) record every change made to files, who made them, and when. This lets you review history, undo mistakes, and collaborate without overwriting each other's work.

questions.question: Git is best described as a:
questions.explanation: Git is a distributed VCS — every developer has a complete copy of the full repository history on their own machine. This means you can work offline and no single server failure loses all history.

questions.question: GitHub is:

options.B: A command-line tool installed on your computer
options.C: A cloud platform that hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration features

questions.explanation: Git is the local tool that tracks changes. GitHub is a website (owned by Microsoft) that hosts your Git repositories online and adds features like pull requests, issues, and GitHub Actions.

questions.question: Who created Git?
questions.explanation: Linus Torvalds created Git in 2005 to manage the Linux kernel source code. He needed a fast, distributed system after the previous tool's free license was revoked.

questions.question: In a distributed version control system like Git, where is the repository stored?

options.C: On every developer's local machine as a full copy

questions.explanation: In a distributed VCS, every developer clones the full repository including its entire history to their own computer. This enables offline work and means there is no single point of failure.

questions.question: Which of the following is a problem that version control solves?

options.B: Two developers accidentally overwriting each other's changes

questions.explanation: Without version control, teams often face lost work when two people edit the same file simultaneously. Git tracks who changed what and helps merge those changes safely.

questions.question: What does a 'repository' (repo) contain?

options.A: Only the latest version of your project files
options.B: Your project files plus the complete history of every change ever made

questions.explanation: A repository stores your project files AND Git's complete history — every commit, branch, and tag. This is what makes it possible to travel back in time to any previous state.

questions.question: Which of these is an alternative to GitHub for hosting Git repositories?
questions.explanation: GitLab is a major GitHub alternative. Others include Bitbucket and Gitea. All of them host Git repositories but Git itself works independently of any hosting platform.

questions.question: If GitHub shuts down tomorrow, what happens to your local Git repository?

options.A: All history is lost because it was stored on GitHub
options.B: Nothing — your local copy still has the full history
options.C: Git stops working on your computer
options.D: Your commits are automatically moved to GitLab

questions.explanation: Because Git is distributed, your local clone contains the entire repository history. GitHub going offline only means you lose the remote copy — your local history stays intact.

questions.question: Which statement about Git commits is correct?

options.A: A commit saves only the files that are currently open in your editor
options.B: A commit is a snapshot of your project at a specific point in time
options.C: A commit automatically uploads your code to GitHub
options.D: You can only make one commit per project

questions.explanation: A commit is Git's way of saving a snapshot of your staged changes with a message describing what changed. Each commit has a unique ID and is linked to the previous commit, forming the project history.
